analysis.one_liner: Charged tobacco companies hundreds of billions to fund children's health and cut youth smoking.
analysis.headline: The Healthy Kids Act, which would have charged tobacco companies $16 billion up front and roughly $24 to $30 billion a year to fund children's health programs and cut youth smoking, never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made tobacco manufacturers pay $16 billion up front, sized by their stock market value, and roughly $24 to $30 billion every year based on their sales, to fund children's health programs. It would have raised cigarette prices by at least $1.50 a pack, given the FDA full authority to regulate tobacco, banned most tobacco advertising, and penalized companies if youth smoking did not fall. The money would have gone to child care, smaller elementary school classes, Medicaid and children's health insurance enrollment, medical research, quit-smoking programs, and aid to tobacco farmers. The bill was referred to eight House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face far fewer cigarettes and ads aimed at them; taxpayers, who would be reimbursed for Medicaid and Medicare costs of treating tobacco-related illness; low-income families, who would get child care funding and smaller first-through-third-grade classes; uninsured and underinsured people with tobacco-related illness, who would get assistance; Medicare patients with cancer, who would get coverage of routine care costs in clinical trials; lawfully present immigrant children, who would become eligible for Medicaid and CHIP; and NIH researchers and state anti-smoking programs, all funded by the tobacco assessments.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a HEALTHY Kids Trust Fund seeded with a $16 billion up-front charge on tobacco makers (split by stock market value) plus annual assessments of roughly $24.3 to $29.9 billion a year based on domestic sales, designed to raise cigarette prices by at least $1.50 a pack to discourage youth purchases.

Funds child care and early childhood development grants, and grants to hire qualified elementary school teachers to cut class sizes in grades 1-3 to no more than 18 students, with priority to high-poverty schools.

Reimburses states for Medicaid costs of treating tobacco-related illness and money to local governments, expands presumptive Medicaid eligibility so schools, child care agencies, and housing agencies can enroll kids, lets states cover lawfully present immigrant children, and rewards states that enroll eligible but unenrolled children with a higher federal match.

Gives the FDA full jurisdiction over tobacco as drugs and devices, authorizing nicotine limits, ingredient disclosure, new warnings, recall authority, and black-text-only advertising; bans outdoor, billboard, cartoon, Internet, and event-sponsorship advertising; and imposes escalating penalties on manufacturers that miss mandatory youth-smoking reduction targets.

Funds research, cessation programs, counter-advertising, assistance for people with tobacco-related illness who are uninsured or underinsured, smoke-free policies in public buildings, and transition payments and retraining for tobacco farmers, factory workers, and their communities.

Requires tobacco companies to hand over internal documents about health effects, addiction, nicotine manipulation, and youth marketing for public disclosure, with only narrow trade-secret and attorney-client exemptions.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers pay the $16 billion initial charge and the annual assessments (about $24 to $30 billion a year), penalties for missing youth-smoking targets, and the cost of an asbestos trust, none of it deductible from taxes or payable from liability insurance. The cost would largely be passed to consumers through the intended $1.50-per-pack price increase, falling on adult smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income. Broadcasters and advertising businesses would lose tobacco ad revenue, and tobacco growers would see demand fall (offset by transition payments).

drawbacks.text: The intended price increase of at least $1.50 a pack is paid by adult smokers, who are disproportionately lower-income, so a large share of the funding would come regressively from working smokers rather than from company profits.

To receive the money, states must dismiss their pending lawsuits against tobacco companies and agree not to file new ones, and manufacturers get consent decrees and a binding National Tobacco Control Protocol that resolves claims for pre-enactment conduct; the tobacco asbestos trust would also bar civil suits against tobacco companies for any person compensated by the trust, trading away some legal accountability for the funding.

Manufacturers that had already settled with more than 25 states before 1998 are exempt from the initial payment and the state-portion of annual assessments, favoring the largest firms that had cut early deals.

If youth-smoking targets are missed, companies owe escalating, multiplied penalties and eventually face generic-packaging mandates — a design that guarantees large annual payments but means the money flows even when prevention fails, and the cost can be passed on in prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits were large and concrete: a major funding stream for child care, smaller early-grade classes, children's health enrollment, medical research, and quitting programs, plus the strongest advertising restrictions and FDA authority ever put before Congress, all paid for by the industry causing the harm. The serious costs are real: the funding is regressive because it comes from higher prices paid by lower-income adult smokers, and the bill buys industry peace by extinguishing state lawsuits and part of private liability, including through an asbestos trust that ends suits by compensated claimants. On balance the bill's design tilts toward the public, but the liability givebacks and the carve-out for early-settling manufacturers are concessions a fair reader could object to.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to eight House committees, then bounced to four subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Vic Fazio introduced the Healthy Kids Act on March 17, 1998, with 45 original cosponsors including House Democratic leaders Richard Gephardt and David Bonior; 54 members cosponsored in total, 53 Democrats and the chamber's one Independent.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to eight committees at once — Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, Agriculture, Budget, Resources, and International Relations.

Between April 7 and April 29, 1998, it was referred to four subcommittees (Risk Management and Specialty Crops; Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection; Health and Environment; International Economic Policy and Trade).

No committee ever reported the bill, no vote was ever taken in committee or on the House floor, and the congressional record shows no further action before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: by dying without a vote, the bill never imposed its $16 billion initial charge, its roughly $24-30 billion in annual assessments, its mandatory youth-smoking penalties, or its advertising bans, and the industry kept its marketing practices and faced no new federal regulation from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred to test the split: all 54 cosponsors were Democrats or the House's single Independent, and no Republican supported the bill on the record, while the Republican majority simply never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have taken roughly $16 billion up front plus $24-30 billion a year from the companies, banned most of their advertising, put them under FDA regulation, and penalized them for missing youth-smoking targets — but it also offered real gains: resolution of state lawsuits, consent decrees and a national protocol limiting liability for past conduct, an asbestos trust that would bar suits by compensated claimants, and an exemption from the initial payment for firms that had already settled with 25-plus states. The industry opposed comprehensive tobacco legislation in 1998 rather than accept the deal.

Title IV would have created a Tobacco Transition Trust Fund paying quota holders for lost crop value, funding community economic development, retraining for producers and factory workers, scholarships, and crop insurance, and would have required cigarette makers to buy minimum quantities of domestic flue-cured and Burley tobacco.

The bill bans tobacco advertising on electronic media and the Internet, outdoors, and in stadiums, restricts print ads to black text on white, and ends branded event sponsorship — removing a lucrative category of ad spending because it was shown to recruit underage smokers.

Tobacco company assessments would fund two asbestos trusts: Fund I would credit asbestos defendants and trusts for tobacco-caused portions of claims already paid, and Fund II would pay future claims — with a release barring civil suits against tobacco companies for anyone compensated, shifting money from tobacco to asbestos claimants.
